notes:
Below are verse-by-verse notes on Isaiah 2. I've labelled each commentator's tradition (Calvin as Reformed, Gill and Spurgeon as Baptist, Clarke as Methodist and so on) from general knowledge. The pages don't state these labels.

**Missing:** I ran out of search and fetch calls before I could get to some of the sites. I found nothing from newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org, bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org, the Lutheran sites, the Pentecostal sites other than Enduring Word, or any page on prosperity or hyper-grace teaching, so those views are left out.

---

**v. 1**
- David Guzik says Isaiah received the message as a kind of vision, because it was a word that he "saw." The prophecy, which runs on through chapter 4, is aimed at Judah and its capital, Jerusalem. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-2/
- Verses 1–3 are repeated in Micah 4:1–3. Guzik says the same Spirit gave both prophets the same vision to establish and emphasise His word. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-2/
- Who borrowed from whom is debated. Barnes says many of the older theologians supposed that the passages were communicated alike by the Holy Spirit to both writers. But there is no improbability in supposing that Isaiah may have availed himself of language used by Micah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/2-2.htm Clarke (Methodist) thinks the reverse: Micah began prophesying later, so Micah probably took it from Isaiah. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/isaiah-2.html
- Bob Utley (bible.org) calls the way revelation came to Isaiah ("he saw") a mystery. He says the key rule for interpretation is the original inspired author's intent: one meaning, but many applications. https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-2

**v. 2**
- **Millennial reading (Guzik, Calvary Chapel):** "The latter days" means the time of the Messiah, which broadly speaks of the millennium. In that time Israel will be the world's leading nation, and the temple mount will be the capital of the Messiah's government. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-2/ Ironside (Brethren, dispensational) holds the same view: in the last days God will take up Israel again and make Jerusalem His throne-city. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/isaiah-2.html
- **Church-age reading:** Matthew Henry sees here the founding of the Christian church: Christianity shall then be the mountain of the Lord's house; where that is professed God will grant his presence. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_002.cfm Gill (Baptist) also takes the "house" to be the kingdom of Christ, which is his church. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/2-2.htm A Henry excerpt on StudyLight adds that the gospel times are the last days. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/2-4.html
- Constable names the divide. He notes that the amillennial interpretation of this passage sees the church as fulfilling what Isaiah wrote of Jerusalem and Judah. He also quotes the view that "the last days" always refers to the furthest point on the speaker's horizon. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/2-4.html
- Calvin (Reformed) admits the vision could look absurd, since Zion was a small hill and Isaiah had just foretold its destruction. https://ccel.org/study/Isaiah_2:2-5
- **More scholarly notes (Utley):**
  - "Last days" can refer to several different periods, and only context decides which. He warns: "Be careful of your systematic theology!"
  - He compares Canaanite myth, where the gods lived on Mount Zaphon, and Mesopotamian texts about raised temples.
  - The Hebrew verb behind "stream" pictures water flowing without end.
  - https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-2

**v. 3**
- Clarke draws lessons from the verse: only God can reveal His will, we should learn it in order to do it, and each person should help a neighbour into that light. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/isaiah-2.html
- Utley says "paths" stands for a way of life lived in obedience, which became the first name of the church: "The Way." https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-2
- Gill sees the "law from Zion" as the gospel, which went out from Jerusalem through Christ and the apostles. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/2-2.htm

**v. 4** *(the verse where views differ most)*
- **Millennial, imposed peace (Guzik):** War ends because the Messiah rules, not because human hearts change. He calls it not the peace of surrender. This is the peace of enforced righteousness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-2/ Ironside says the nations do not beat swords into plowshares now, but only when Christ returns to take David's throne. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/isaiah-2.html
- **Reformed (Calvin):** Calvin sees this as the result of Christ bringing the nations under His rule. He sharply rejects a pacifist reading: Some madmen torture this passage to promote anarchy, as if it banned all use of the sword. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/2-4.html
- **Matthew Henry:** He links the peace to the success of the gospel, but says the verse does not make all war absolutely unlawful among Christians, nor is it a prophecy that in the days of the Messiah there shall be no wars. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/2-4.html
- **Coffman:** He calls the "universal peace on earth" reading totally in error and cites Matthew 24:6. Following Homer Hailey, he says the kingdom is not spread by physical weapons. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/2-4.html
- **Pulpit Commentary:** This is clearly not yet fulfilled. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/2-4.htm
- **Ellicott** hopes for a partial, "germinant" fulfilment within history. The Cambridge Bible says the meaning is that disputes are taken to Jehovah, whose judgment is accepted as final. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/2-4.htm
- **Background:**
  - Barnes says the Syrian plowshare looked so much like a short sword that one could easily be turned into the other.
  - Ellicott notes the words reverse Joel 3:10.
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/2-4.htm
  - Clarke cites Roman poets (Martial, Virgil, Ovid) who used the same picture, and laments that war is taught as a trade. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/isaiah-2.html

**v. 5**
- Guzik: after painting the Messiah's reign, Isaiah calls Judah to live under it now. He adds that walking in the light means enjoying the blessings of that reign today, and quotes Spurgeon's advice to travel to heaven "first-class." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-2/
- Utley sees a deliberate parallel: in v. 3 it is the nations speaking, and in v. 5 it is Israel. https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-2

**v. 6**
- Precept Austin says the whole section from 2:6 to 4:1 gives God's reason for forsaking His people. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_25-9_commentary
- Guzik: Judah had let foreign false gods capture its attention. He says this is not a statement against immigrants or other cultures. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-2/
- Coffman reads "strike hands with foreigners" as business partnerships, marriages and other close ties with idolatrous nations. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/2-5.html
- Henry says Judah copied eastern customs and thought that conforming made them more refined. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/2-9.html
- Clarke notes problems in the Hebrew text. He proposes the reading "with divination from the east," and an alternative meaning for "replenished": joining with foreigners in marriage or worship. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/isaiah-2.html

**v. 7**
- Clarke: the horses and gold directly broke Deuteronomy 17:16–17. He thinks Uzziah followed Solomon's example after recovering the port of Elath. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/isaiah-2.html
- Henry says God wanted Israel to depend on Him alone, but they felt they needed treasure and chariots to match their neighbours. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/2-9.html
- Guzik: this is not a rebuke of wealth itself, but of loving and trusting riches. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-2/

**v. 8**
- Clarke points out that Uzziah and Jotham are said to have done right. He therefore suggests these were private household idols, such as teraphim used for divination. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/isaiah-2.html
- Guzik: this is not a rebuke of work, but of worshipping what we have made. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-2/

**v. 9** *("do not forgive them")*
- **Prayer or prediction?**
  - Barnes says the Hebrew future has the force of a command, a threat spoken to God.
  - Ellicott prefers "thou canst not forgive them."
  - Keil & Delitzsch: God neither could nor would forgive this time.
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/2-9.htm
  - The Pulpit Commentary also says it means "thou canst not forgive them." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-46.html
  - Constable: Isaiah was not asking God to refrain from forgiving His people. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/2-9.html
- **Calvin** says it makes little difference which reading you take. He adds that Isaiah tacitly leaves room for a remnant, because he speaks of the nation as a whole. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/2-9.html
- **Henry** applies it to the nation, not individuals (many repented and were pardoned). He sees Babylon as a type of the final destruction by the Romans. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_002.cfm
- **Coffman** sees "judicial hardening" here. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/2-9.html
- **Precept Austin** holds that no one is beyond God's forgiveness, yet hearts can become so hardened that this cry is warranted. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_25-9_commentary
- **Gill** reads it prophetically of worshippers of the beast (Revelation 14:9). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/2-9.html
- **Barnes and JFB:** "mean man" and "great man" mean all ranks of people. All of them were idolaters. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/2-9.htm
- **Guzik:** Judah knew how to bow down, but bowed to the wrong things. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-2/

**v. 10**
- Precept Austin: here hiding is commanded, and in vv. 19 and 21 it is foretold. The command was partly fulfilled in Babylon's destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BC, and will be fulfilled worldwide in the Tribulation. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_210-12_commentary
- Clarke adds the line "When he ariseth to strike the earth with terror," following the Septuagint (the ancient Greek translation). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/isaiah-2.html

**v. 11**
- Utley: "in that day" points back to the last days of v. 2. https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-2
- Constable quotes the view that pride and ambition are humanity's most devastating sins, and that idolatry is one way man tries to exalt himself. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/2-9.html

**v. 12**
- Guzik: the "day of the LORD" is not necessarily a single day but "God's time." He sets it against the present "day of man." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-2/
- Bridgeway: Israel hoped God would act against its enemies, but before He does, He must act against Israel. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/2-9.html

**vv. 13–16**
- Clarke reads these as metaphors:
  - Cedars and oaks stand for kings and princes.
  - Mountains stand for kingdoms.
  - Towers stand for defenders.
  - Ships of Tarshish stand for wealthy merchants.
  - He identifies Tarshish as probably Tartessus in Spain.
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/isaiah-2.html
- Henry: the day of the Lord falls on the very things they trusted in. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/2-19.html
- Guzik sees towers and ships as expressions of human pride. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-2/

**vv. 17–18**
- Bridgeway: neither arrogant self-confidence nor devotion to idols will save them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/2-9.html
- Clarke notes a textual point: old versions read "shall disappear" as a plural verb. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/isaiah-2.html

**v. 19**
- The Cambridge Bible hears an echo of the great earthquake in Uzziah's reign, which Isaiah probably lived through. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/2-19.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch say Revelation 6:15 shows this describes the last judgment, but "bounded by a national horizon." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/2-19.htm
- Poole takes the shaking as more probably figurative, meaning dreadful judgments. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/2-19.htm By contrast, the BibleHub study note says the Creator will literally rock the planet. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/2-19.htm
- Barnes: Judea's caves were natural refuges in war, so this was a natural picture of panic. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/2-19.html
- Chuck Smith links this to the sixth seal in Revelation. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/2-19.html

**v. 20**
- Clarke heads vv. 18–21 as the complete destruction of idolatry that follows the setting up of Messiah's kingdom. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/isaiah-2.html
- A BibleHub excerpt (author not named) says covetous men make money their god, but will one day find it a burden. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/2-19.htm

**v. 21**
- Calvin: v. 10 addressed the people directly ("you"), to strike them harder. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/2-19.html
- Henry: it is useless to seek refuge in caves when the earth itself is shaken. The only shelter is in God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/2-19.html

**v. 22**
- **Is the verse original?** It is missing from the Septuagint, and some critics call it a later margin note.
  - Ellicott answers that it is the natural close of the discourse.
  - The Pulpit Commentary says that if it is kept, it calls Israel to give up the trust in man from which all their other errors flowed.
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/2-22.htm
- **"Breath in his nostrils":**
  - Calvin: man's life is a breath that vanishes at once. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/2-22.html
  - Barnes applies it to salvation: only God can save from the day of wrath. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/2-22.htm
- **Spurgeon (Baptist):** man is frail, changeable and fearful. The verse implies we are already too entangled with men and must stop idolising them. https://www.spurgeon.org/resource-library/sermons/man-whose-breath-is-in-his-nostrils/
- **Gill** uniquely reads "that man" as the antichrist. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/2-22.html
- **Guzik** applies it to caring too much about people's opinions. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-2/
- **Catholic text history:** The Douay-Rheims reads the end as "for he is reputed high." https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/rhe/isaiah/2-22.html Keil & Delitzsch say this goes back to Jerome's mistaken vowel-pointing, by which Luther was apparently misled. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/2-22.htm
